conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the bariatric team doctors. You came in tonight because of low blood sugar—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up this morning feeling really shaky and confused. My glucose monitor alarm went off—it said my blood sugar was 43.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s quite low. Did you treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took my sugar pills right away. I felt better after a few minutes, but then it happened again later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. We’re going to keep an eye on your levels. You also mentioned increased drainage around your G-tube and some pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the site has been leaking more than usual. I’m changing the dressing twice a day now because it gets soaked. And it’s tender—more than normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that. We’ve ordered a scan to make sure your tube is still in the right place and not leaking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it possible the feeds are backing up into the bag? I’ve been worried the pump isn’t delivering them properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. The scan will help us see how the contrast moves. If it’s refluxing, we’ll adjust your setup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your abdominal X-ray with contrast shows the G-tube is correctly placed in the stomach. No leakage outside the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube is okay? But why am I having these lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube is working, but we think your hypoglycemia might be related to bacterial overgrowth in your intestines. You’ve had that before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from my breath test. So that could be causing the lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Bacteria can ferment carbs and trigger insulin release. We’re restarting your Flagyl to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the soreness at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some granulation tissue—extra tissue that sometimes grows around tubes. It can cause irritation and drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s common. We’ll treat it with silver nitrate to reduce it and prescribe an ointment called Bactroban to prevent infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugars have been stable overnight—between 80 and 110. No episodes of hypoglycemia so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean the Flagyl is working already?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s early, but staying on your feeds and being in a controlled setting helps. Your endocrinologist wants a fasting test to check what’s driving the insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fasting test? But I need my tube feeds to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it carefully. We’ll stop the feeds and monitor your blood sugar every hour. When it drops to around 55, we’ll draw blood to check insulin, C-peptide, and other levels, then restart your feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And that will tell us why I’m having lows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It helps distinguish if it’s from too much insulin production, reactive hypoglycemia, or something else. Your endocrinologist will review the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the fasting test this morning. You went about 12 hours without feeds. Your blood sugar dropped to 55, and we got the labs right then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did I do? Did I pass out or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you stayed alert the whole time. Nurses checked you every hour. All the labs were sent to your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And the contrast study this morning—what did that show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The contrast moved all the way into your colon and rectum. That means your digestive tract is open and functioning—no blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So everything’s moving like it should?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your tube site is looking better after treatment. We’ll keep using the silver nitrate and Bactroban ointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Another good night—your sugars stayed between 55 and 110. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your tube feeds as before. Take Flagyl three times a day for the bacterial overgrowth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds—octreotide and acarbose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Octreotide helps reduce insulin spikes, and acarbose slows sugar absorption. They may help prevent lows after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And for the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Apply the Bactroban ointment twice a day to the granulation tissue. Keep the dressing clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I have my follow-up with Dr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll review your test results and adjust your plan if needed. We’ll send them all the labs from the fasting test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—vitals stable, sugars in range. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any last instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds as prescribed. Use glucose tablets if your sugar drops. And call if you have fever, redness, or increased pain at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel shaky again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your sugar. If it’s low, treat it with glucose and sit down. If it doesn’t improve, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I feel much better knowing we’re on top of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send prescriptions for Flagyl, Bactroban, and the new meds. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one more thing—should I keep checking my blood sugar at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially before meals and at bedtime. And any time you feel shaky or confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.
